title: Cotton-Candy Worlds: Astronomers Discover Two Unbelievably Fluffy Planets
summary: Imagine a planet so light it could float on water — if you could find an ocean big enough. An international team led by the University of Oxford has confirmed two such worlds, TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, which boast the lowest densities ever recorded for giant planets. Their densities — 0.038 and 0.047 grams per cubic centimeter — are less than that of cotton candy (0.05 g/cm³) and a staggering 28 to 35 times lower than Jupiter's 1.33 g/cm³. Earth, by comparison, is a dense 5.5 g/cm³. These "super-puff" planets orbit an F7-type dwarf star about 1,110 light-years away in the constellation Volans. They are locked in a rare 5:3 mean-motion resonance: for every five orbits of the inner planet, the outer completes three. This gravitational dance causes measurable transit-timing variations, which allowed astronomers to calculate their masses. The discovery began with citizen scientists. Volunteers in the Planet Hunters TESS project flagged the planets in 2019 and 2023 after poring over data from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite. Follow-up observations spanned eight years, including crucial data from the ASTEP telescope at Concordia Station in Antarctica. There, months of uninterrupted winter darkness enabled continuous monitoring of the planets' transits, each lasting over 11 hours — the longest continuous planetary transits ever fully observed from the ground. Lead author Dr. [name redacted] said, "Only a handful of these super-puffy planets are known, and it is even rarer to find two in the same system. Their extremely low densities make them fascinating targets for understanding how planetary systems form and evolve." Scientists suspect these planets possess enormous atmospheres of hydrogen and helium, possibly accreted far from the star in colder regions of the protoplanetary disc. Only four other systems are known to host multiple super-puffs, making TOI-791 an exceptional laboratory. Future observations aim to probe their atmospheres and test competing formation theories, potentially reshaping our understanding of planetary diversity.
why_it_matters: Studying extreme planets like these helps us understand the full range of possible worlds. It challenges the idea that our solar system is typical, and the knowledge gained could one day help us recognise signs of life on a variety of planet types.

background_read: NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS, launched in 2018) scans the whole sky for tiny dips in starlight caused by planets crossing in front of their stars. The data is so vast that the Planet Hunters TESS project (a citizen-science program on the Zooniverse platform) asks volunteers to help identify promising signals.

The ASTEP telescope (Antarctic Search for Transiting ExoPlanets) sits at Concordia Station, a French-Italian research base on the Antarctic Plateau. The site's long, dark winter allows telescopes to stare at the same star for weeks without interruption — perfect for catching very long planetary transits that would be broken up by daylight at other observatories.

Mean-motion resonances are not just orbital curiosities; they can reveal how planetary systems evolved. For example, Jupiter's moons Io, Europa, and Ganymede are in a 4:2:1 resonance, and their gravitational tugs cause tidal heating that powers volcanic activity. Finding a 5:3 resonance in a distant system gives clues to how planets migrate and settle into stable orbits.

Only four other star systems are known to host multiple super-puffs. This rarity makes TOI-791 an important laboratory for testing theories of how such lightweight worlds form — perhaps they started with much larger cores and slowly lost mass, or they formed late when the protoplanetary disc was almost gone.

perspectives.description: Finding super-puffs expands our imagination about what planets can be like. The involvement of citizen scientists shows that the public can directly contribute to major discoveries, making astronomy more democratic.

So few of these systems are known that we might be drawing conclusions from a tiny, biased sample. The planets' low densities also make them very fragile — their atmospheres could be stripped away by their star's radiation, so they may be short-lived oddities rather than stable members of planetary families.

This discovery is a case study in how modern astronomy blends space telescopes, ground-based facilities in extreme locations, machine-learning algorithms, and human pattern recognition. Each step filters data, and biases in any one part can shape which planets we find.

Instruments like the James Webb Space Telescope could analyse the atmospheres of these planets and reveal what gases they contain. If their atmospheres are enriched in water vapour, that might hint at an origin farther out in the disc, testing our models of planet migration.
